lesson.title: The Protocol That Holds the Internet Together: BGP
lesson.summary: BGP is the real path vector protocol that runs between autonomous systems across the internet, selecting routes by policy and business relationships rather than by shortest path alone.
lesson.body:
BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, is path vector routing put into practice as the single protocol that actually runs the internet's interdomain routing. Every major network that makes up the internet speaks BGP to its neighboring networks, and the sum of all those BGP sessions, exchanging routes hop by hop across organizational boundaries, is what allows a packet to find its way from a home network in one country to a server operated by a completely unrelated organization on another continent, despite no single entity ever having configured that end to end path directly. Like OSPF, BGP, currently version four, is an open standard, documented in RFC 4271, which matters for the same reason OSPF being open matters: no single vendor or single network controls how the entire internet routes traffic.

The mechanics follow the path vector pattern described earlier, but it is worth making the contrast with OSPF's link state approach explicit, because the two protocols solve superficially similar problems, getting a packet to the right destination, in almost opposite ways. An OSPF router floods its link costs to every router in its network and expects every router to end up with an identical full topology map. A BGP router does no flooding at all. It opens a direct, explicitly configured connection, over TCP on port 179, to each neighboring router it wants to exchange routes with, called a peer, and advertises routes only to those specific peers. Each route advertisement carries a destination prefix and the AS path, the ordered list of autonomous system numbers the route has crossed so far, along with other attributes, rather than a link cost. A BGP router never sees the internet's full topology the way an OSPF router sees its domain's full topology, it only ever sees, for each destination prefix, a handful of candidate paths offered by its immediate peers, each labeled with the sequence of networks it would cross.

Choosing among those candidate paths is where BGP most clearly departs from shortest path routing. BGP does not simply pick the route with the fewest AS hops. It runs a route selection process that considers business and policy factors first, commonly things like preferring routes learned from a customer over routes learned from a peer or a provider, because carrying customer traffic is what a network is paid to do, applying locally configured preferences, and only falling back to AS path length as one of several tiebreakers. Two networks connected by BGP might route traffic along a path with more AS hops than an alternative simply because that path is cheaper, more reliable, or matches a business agreement, something that would be meaningless to express in OSPF's pure cost minimizing world, but is completely ordinary in BGP's policy driven one. Internally within a large network, routers also run BGP among themselves, called interior BGP, specifically so that routes learned at one edge of the network via external BGP sessions with other autonomous systems can be distributed to every other router that needs to forward traffic toward them, while the network's actual internal forwarding still relies on an interior protocol like OSPF to get packets to the right exit point.
